paragraphs.text: Everywhere, and in practically all of the divine narratives, words fall short of the realities and language is weaker than its subject, but this is especially true of the achievements of blessed Job. No one could ever make the speech of his own poverty equal to the account his subject deserves. Even if countless things are said about him, the speech still falls short of the power that would do him justice. Since, then, we have already said what we could, in a modest way, nothing prevents us from taking up the same narratives again today. And let no one think the subject is insulted if we cut the narrative into pieces. Job feels no pain at being cut. If he felt no pain when his body was cut, will he feel pain when his story is cut? We learned from the earlier narratives that he lost everything, or rather that he found everything. For although he lost all that was bright, he did not lose the root of brightness. He lost the lyre, but the craftsman remained; he lost the fruits of abundance, but the farmer of prosperity remained; he was stripped of all his possessions, but he was not stripped of virtue. He threw his possessions to the devil, casting away his livelihood, as Joseph left his cloak with the shameless woman. In suffering he did not suffer. We must both acknowledge the suffering of nature and sing the praises of the soul's courage. The marks of nature were shown, and the superior strength of virtue was shown as well. He heard of the calamity that had befallen his children and tore his garments, to show the fellow-feeling of nature. If he had not suffered, he would not have been admired as a lover of virtue; he would have been condemned as unfeeling. But he suffered as a man and endured as a lover of God. He laid bare the weakness of nature and did not betray the way of piety. He tore his garments, but he worshipped. So the devil did not strike as much as he was struck, and did not wound as much as he was wounded. Yet when Job had fought the first contest well, God put him into another contest, so as to weave him a more brilliant crown of endurance. For a second time the angels present themselves, and the devil is questioned in their midst by the One who knows all things: "Where do you come from?" See the wisdom of God, see the cunning of the devil. God knew where he came from: he came defeated by the righteous man. But God wants to see whether he will honestly admit his defeat. "Where have you come from?" The devil hides his defeat, for he was ashamed, and uses the same words as the first time: "I am here after going around the earth and walking about under heaven." Is that what you went out for? Is that what you asked for? Did you not say, "Hand Job's possessions over to me"? Why do you hide the contest? Is it to make the crown of victory disappear? Tell of the contest, accursed one, tell of the wrestling as well, so that you may proclaim the victory! But what the devil hid out of envy, the Master of all proclaims in praise of the man's virtuous wisdom. "Have you set your mind against my servant?" What you hide, I make known. God often asks questions, not to learn something, but to exercise the disposition of those he questions and see whether they will honestly confess. So he asked Cain, "Where is Abel your brother?" He wanted the one who had done the evil at least to stand up as his own accuser, so that his self-accusation might lessen the gravity of the crime. For anyone who accuses himself softens the judge's anger. Then he asked Cain, "Where is Abel your brother?" Cain thought the question came from ignorance and said, "I do not know. Am I my brother's keeper?" Once God had tested his disposition, he exposed the sacrilege, saying, "The voice of your brother's blood cries out to me from the ground." In the same way, if God asks a question and sees that the person will not be honest, he convicts the wrongdoer. And now, since in questioning the devil he does not hear from him of the defeat he suffered, God himself publicly brands him with his defeat and celebrates the victory of the righteous man: "Have you set your mind against my servant Job, that there is none like him on earth, guileless?" Here, I beg you, pay close attention, and do not pass over the words of the divine Scriptures. In the first testimony the word "guileless" was never spoken; it appears in the second. In the first, God said: "Have you set your mind against my servant Job, that there is no one like him on earth, a man blameless, righteous, true, keeping himself from every evil deed?" He did not add "guileless" there. But after the victory and the contest he adds it for him like a crown, a word of praise in harmony with his feats. He had suffered countless things and borne the calamity guilelessly, without blaspheming against the Master; he had judged everything as goodness and said, "If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, shall we not bear the evil?" Since that saying was a saying of guilelessness, God weaves him a crown of guilelessness: there is no man of his kind so guileless. "And you, why did you say to destroy his possessions for nothing?" That is: you envied his wealth in vain. You said the man was pious for the sake of money. He was stripped of his possessions, and he was not stripped of the truth. So you, devil, said to destroy his possessions for nothing. Wickedness is never at a loss for malice. Once again it finds another insinuation that might quench the virtuous man's courage. So it says to God: "Skin for skin, and all that a man has he will give for his life." It is nothing great, he says, that Job lost his possessions. He gladly despised them all to save himself. "But if you wish to test him, touch his flesh; surely he will bless you to your face." "Bless" stands for "curse," for Scripture has covered the evil word with a word of good omen.

And why was this written? So that you, the believer, may learn to cover the shameful details with decent words when you tell of other people's wrongs. Do not put on airs of propriety while doing shameful things; show your propriety instead by avoiding shameful talk. This is why the apostle says, "Let no shameful word come out of your mouth." Then God hands the contestant over to a second trial. God is not learning from the trial what kind of contestant Job was; he is putting the devil to shame by the trial. For God knows all things before all things. "And the devil went out from the presence of the Lord and struck Job with a malignant sore from his feet to his head." He made his whole body a single wound, a single welt. It was fitting that Job be crowned as a contestant wholly and entirely. From feet to head was the wound that saves, the sore that wins the victory. To the eye the sore ran with pus, but to the understanding it was full of praise. The pus of the sore lasted only a short time, but the praises his contest bore will never be used up for all eternity. "He struck him with a malignant sore from his feet to his head," so that he might be shown to be crowned in every one of his limbs. No place within the walls would take in a man so afflicted in body; every household pushed him out as a leper, for Job's wound was nothing other than leprosy. So he went out of the city, a stranger to the world. He went out of the city and sat on the dunghill. He went out of the city, for his contest was not of this world; it surpassed the present order of things. Being outside the city and outside the wall was an image of the cross of Christ. This is why Paul says: "The bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the sanctuary are burned outside the camp. Therefore Jesus also suffered outside the gate, in order to sanctify the people." Christ was outside the gate; Job, outside the city, sat on the dunghill. He was the seed of piety, the seed of endurance, manured by afflictions, and he sat on the dunghill waiting for the One who "raises the poor from the earth and lifts the needy from the dunghill." Brothers, he saw his body wasting away but his soul standing firm; he saw his body crawling with worms but his soul giving birth to piety; he saw the earthen vessel decaying, and before Paul ever spoke he remembered Paul's words. For it would have been fitting for him to say, "As much as our outer man is decaying, so much is the inner man being renewed day by day." He took a potsherd to scrape off the pus. With the potsherd he scraped off the pus, and with endurance he wore down his opponent. It would have been fitting for him too, holding the potsherd, to say, "We have this treasure in an earthen vessel." The man who had raised many from the dunghill sat on the dunghill; he took a potsherd to scrape off the pus; with dead clay he scraped the living clay. The three friends came, for calamities summon friends to give comfort. Eliphaz, Zophar and Bildad came: three kings to one king. For before this he had been a king, the one who says, "I was among them like a king among his troops." "And they sat," it says, "before Job seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke." Moderate calamities admit of comfort, but great calamities are honored with silence. There are times, brothers, when grief overpowers comfort. Just as diseases at their crisis reject every treatment, so griefs at the height of calamity drive out all counsel. They kept silent, sharing his suffering by their silence. And what does he do? Since the calamity had overcome them and no one dared to break into words of comfort, Job is the first to begin speaking: the sufferer opens the door for those who are not suffering. For we know, brothers, that in calamities, or in mourning, or in any other gloomy situation, each person is reluctant to be the first to speak, so as not to seem an untimely preacher of virtue or of advice; but if he sees someone else begin, he follows without risk. Brothers, experience teaches this, and the facts bear it out. So when he saw that grief had shut out the comfort of his friends, the sufferer opens the door and immediately begins to lament his calamity in tragic terms, while everywhere avoiding any suspicion of blasphemy. Job's first words: "Cursed be the day on which I was born, and that night, may it be darkness." He says this not out of impiety but out of suffering. And see what he does. Think of someone with a terrible abscess who is being cut open with a knife by a doctor. Having no way to resist the one cutting him, he grabs the people around him and bites the bystanders. He has nothing to charge them with, but he does not have the strength to raise his hand against the doctor. So too Job, fearing the enormity of blasphemy, abuses lifeless things and gives full vent to his suffering. He does not dare to speak against God, but accuses himself and the day. He curses not the creation but his own day. "I have authority over my own day," he says. "I do not curse the work of creation; I curse my own day." "Cursed be the day on which I was born, and that night, may it be darkness." Jeremiah says the same: "Woe is me, mother! What kind of man did you bear me to be, judged and put on trial? Cursed be the day on which I was born." The saints lament all these things in tragic terms so that you may learn from them that they did not pass through life in luxury, but went through their contests enduring countless evils. So Jeremiah too wept, saying, "Woe is me, mother! What kind of man did you bear me to be?" He suffered as a man, but endured as a lover of God. In the same way Moses, the great and divine lawgiver of God, who received the sacred tablets, the first to teach what is good for human life, also speaks to God, weighed down by the multitude of his troubles: "Lord, you said, 'You have found favor with me, and I know you above all.' If I have found favor before you, take my life from me, for I cannot bear the burden of this people. A little more and they will stone me. Did I conceive them in labor? Did I give birth to them, that you say to me, 'Carry them as a nurse carries the child'? I cannot bear the failings of this people." Yet even in lamenting and mourning as a man, he did not blaspheme like a godless man; he showed the passions of nature, laid bare by those very passions. Each of the prophets laments in the same way. Habakkuk says, "Why have you shown me toils and troubles, so that I look upon the miseries of men?" The choir of prophets saw injustice and could not bear it, and Habakkuk cried out: "Why have you shown me toils and troubles? Before me there has been a trial, and the judge takes bribes, and so judgment goes out perverted. The ruler asks, and the judge takes, and the law is set at nothing."

In this way all the righteous suffered and chafed at the hardships of the world. But do not take these examples as approving your own inclinations. Do not say, "Am I better than Jeremiah, who cried out against the world?" Do not let words meant for healing become wounds for you. These things were written so that you may learn how great a contest they fought and how full of dangers was the life they passed through. Do you want to learn what you ought to be? Learn what came after grace. The prophets suffered, and the apostles suffered too; but the prophets felt pain in their suffering, while the apostles boasted in theirs. Paul came forward suffering but not weeping, beaten but not lamenting, tortured but boasting. And what does he say? "Not only that, but we also boast in afflictions, knowing that affliction produces endurance, endurance produces proven character, proven character produces hope, and hope does not put us to shame." And again, after they had been beaten, the apostles "went out from the presence of the council rejoicing that they had been counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Christ." So do not take what came before grace as the pattern for life under grace. These things were told to us so that you may learn hope from their labors. In this way Job too curses the day and suffers in his soul, yet he does not torment his soul with impiety. He bears his wounds and does not wound his soul with blasphemy. Now, since we must be brief, we will briefly sum up the subject for you. In Job's contest everyone except God was ignorant of the purpose of the contest. Job did not know what he was contending for; he did not know that these bouts had been set before him as training. The friends did not know God's purpose. The devil did not know the future, for if he had known that he would be defeated, he would not have made the attempt. Job did not know what the outcome of the contest would be. That God had handed him over by way of permission, Job did know, not because he foresaw it, but because he learned it from God. But the devil did not know what end the bouts would come to. If he had known, he would not have made the attempt, so as not to bring a worse shame upon himself. But what happened to him with the martyrs also happened to him with Job. He killed martyrs to extinguish the church, not knowing that after the martyrs the church would flourish. So everyone was ignorant except God. The friends, ignorant of God's purpose and ignorant of Job's testing, were weighing things up in their ignorance, and they chose to condemn Job as suffering what he deserved rather than to find fault with God for judging undeservedly. Pay close attention. They chose to condemn a man as suffering what his sin deserved rather than to say against God that he had judged unjustly. In one respect they hit the mark, in saying that God is free of injustice; in another respect they went astray, in condemning the innocent. But ignorance speaks in defense of the ignorant, and they are to be accepted, because they reason in ignorance and, keeping their eyes on God's justice, they do not cast their vote against it. They set aside Job's righteousness, but they sing the praises of God's. Then Job begins to be reproved by his friends, and they say to him: "When have the true perished root and all? When have you seen the righteous destroyed root and branch?" "If you had not sinned," one says, "and done what deserves the penalty of sin, the Just One would not have wronged you unjustly. Your sins are many. And if you did not sin, where does this come from, unless your sons sinned? Often you wronged a widow and oppressed orphans. If these things happened, then God was just in bringing this sentence on you." Job was conscious that he had done nothing of the kind, and he was equally conscious that God does not judge unjustly. So when Job saw that men had condemned him, while his conscience did not condemn him and his God found no fault with him, and since he could not persuade men, he turns his words to the Judge and lifts the eye of his soul on high, not blaspheming but pleading, and says to him: "You who know the mind of men, why have you made me your accuser?" You have made me plead against your own justice; you know my heart. Then Job utters something bold, not out of malice but out of guilelessness. To compress much into a few words, since the material of his pleading is vast, he says: "Who will provide a judge between me and you, to find out how many my sins are, that you have judged me like this?" The words are fearsome, but they come from guilelessness. For God had said beforehand that there was none guileless like him, and no one counts a guileless man's words as wickedness. Brothers, all of us human beings, to say nothing of God, always judge not by the deeds themselves but by the intention of those who do them. A son insults his father, and the thing is intolerable both to the one who suffers it and to the one who hears of it. Such a son is called a parricide and a matricide, impious and lawless, because he uttered words against his father and dared to speak ill of his own root. All this befalls the one who has reached mature reason, and he is condemned. But an innocent little child, even if he strikes his father or mother or even insults them, is dearer than any delight. Mothers often provoke their children to insult them, delighting not in the insult but in the innocence, the purity and the simplicity of their character. So too God, knowing that Job speaks not out of malice but out of guilelessness (for he bears witness to him, saying, "He still holds fast to his guilelessness"), accepts Job's words when Job summons him to judgment. These are fearsome words: a servant summoning his master to judgment, a man summoning God, the creature its Creator, the clay the one who formed it. Nevertheless, as I said before, these are words of guilelessness, not of wickedness. Yet, brothers, this guilelessness was not without understanding; it was within the bounds of all wisdom. Do you want to learn this more precisely? Job asked for nothing that he had not done himself. He knew that he was God's servant, and he knew that God was his master. But he himself had often been in disputes with his own slaves and had granted them the dignity of an equal right to speak. If ever a slave brought a case against him, he did not silence him as a slave but heard his plea. What he had done, he asked for, trusting in the saying, "With the measure you measure, it will be measured back to you." And he says, "Who will provide a judge?" And when did you keep an equal right to speak for a slave? Listen to him as he lists his virtues, saying this not out of vanity but out of guilelessness: "I did not reject the cause of my manservant or my maidservant when they contended with me. I will give an answer to God. Was he not formed as I was?" With these thoughts in mind, he granted the common right of free speech to the nature they shared in common.

But we, brothers, are not like that. Do you admire the righteous man? Then condemn yourself. For often, when someone brings a charge (I don't mean against a slave, but against someone a little beneath him) and that person answers with what is just, he silences him as shameless, as someone who dares to speak as an equal. "So you actually dare," he says, "to speak to me as an equal? You demand what is just?" Accept the just right of the other to speak as an equal! The proud man brings a charge and neither accepts a defense nor is moved by silence. If the accused keeps silent, he says, "He stands convicted; he cannot even open his lips." If he speaks, he says, "He dared to raise his voice against his master." Then another man, full of pride, is urged for justice's sake and on behalf of a noble man, and is begged to come to terms with the other, to make peace and to put an end to the malice with love. At once, carried away by pride, he says, "Am I to come down to his level?" Oh, what pride! Where are you standing, that you should come down? "Am I to come down to his level?" He speaks as though he walked on heaven and the clouds. You walk on the same earth, you are fed from the same earth, you return to it, you are buried in it. So where are you coming down from? Are you not ashamed? Do you not stand in awe of the Lord's passion? Are you not ashamed to say to your equal, "Am I to come down to this?" Are you not ashamed to say such things, knowing that Jesus came down for your sake? Against such attitudes and such pride we should always cry out with Isaiah: "Why are earth and ashes proud?" But let us return to our subject: "Who will provide a judge between me and you?" In the end the righteous Judge appears, and he appears to him out of the whirlwind and the clouds. He who was about to pour out the rain of blessing appears to Job from the clouds. He who was about to water the seed lying in the dung appears to him out of the clouds. He raises Job up: he only nods, and the sufferings are scattered; he only nods, and he raises the fallen man and says to him: "Arise, and gird up your loins like a man. I will question you, and you answer me. Since you have called me to judgment and said, 'Who will provide a judge between me and you?', arise, noble contender, you who did not fall under the blow of calamity. Arise!" For if someone is disciplined and bears the calamity and the discipline nobly, he hears from God the word "Arise," as when he says to Jerusalem: "Arise, Jerusalem, you who have drunk the cup of my wrath." "Gird up your loins like a man. I will question you, and you answer me." He did not say, "I will judge you, and you answer me." For he says: "You did not call me to judgment; you called me to be judged alongside you. You asked for a judge between me and you: you be the judge. Do you think I have dealt with you for any other reason than that you might be shown to be righteous?" He means: "Do you suppose I brought this calamity on you for any other reason than to show you to be righteous?" And look closely at how precise these words are. He did not say, "Do you think I have dealt with you for any other reason than that you might become righteous?" For the calamity did not make him righteous; it made his righteousness known. "Do you think I have dealt with you for any other reason than that you might be shown to be righteous? To me," he says, "you were known even before the contests, but to the world you are made known through the calamity; through the wrestling match you are proclaimed to the world. That is why I dealt with you this way: not to harm you but to crown you, not to put you to shame but to make you glorious. But since in your innocence you went beyond the limits of your nature, I have pardoned your simplicity." For even if someone sins out of innocence, God corrects what is done out of innocence. "Since you went so far as to call God to judgment, tell me: what equality with me did you have when you called me? Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth? Were you a contemporary of the Maker, that you should call him to judgment? He was before the ages, and you came many ages later. When I was fashioning the earth, you were not there; when I made the sea, you were not there; nor were you there for anything else of that kind. The whole creation came into being, and you were nowhere. So have you called to judgment the one who is older than the ages, the Creator of all that was made? When I stretched the measuring line over the earth, when I set its pillars firm, when I brought the sea out of its mother's womb, when the sea was being born, where were you? When I covered it with a cloud and wrapped it in mist, where were you?" He takes him to task for having spoken unfittingly: out of innocence, it is true, but also out of ignorance. And what does he do? He does not rebuke him in front of everyone, but corrects him privately, as a friend. When he had said these things and others like them (there is no time to explain every phrase in detail), Job came to know himself, for the righteous man corrects his fault at the first rebuke. And he says: "Lord, before, I had heard of you with the hearing of my ear, but now my eye has seen you, and I have despised myself, and I count myself dust and ashes." And: "I have spoken once; I will not add a second time." See how the man who took the reproof well takes back his fault. "I have spoken once," and that out of innocence, not out of wickedness; "I will not add a second time. For who am I, to be judged before the Lord?" What Job did not know beforehand because of his innocence, he learns after the rebuke. Then what does God do? He does not let him withdraw from the trial, but says: "No; gird up your loins like a man." "Stand like a man," he says. "Do not think that I overwhelmed you with my power in order to escape what is just. I only corrected your simplicity. But I do not withdraw from the trial: judge me justly, and demand an account of what has happened. You were put on trial so that you might be crowned; you were put on trial so that you might be admired throughout the whole world under heaven. Before your suffering one corner of the earth knew you; after your suffering the whole world under heaven will know you. Your dunghill has become more splendid than any royal crown. Those who wear the crown long to see your contest and the toil of your struggles. I have made your dunghill a paradise; I have cultivated it for godliness; I have raised up a heavenly plant. You have received the heavenly things; receive the earthly ones too. Receive everything twice over." Learn from this, every Christian, what your hope is, how far your promise surpasses his. For to Job he promises double, and gives double, but the Savior says to his disciples: "Whoever has left father or mother or sisters for my sake will receive a hundredfold and will inherit eternal life." But notice carefully how he corrects his friend privately, while he rebukes Job's friends openly. God says to them: "Why did you not speak rightly against my servant Job?" "But, righteous Judge, we spoke on your behalf! We proclaimed your justice; we condemned a man and showed your justice to be blameless." Here, then, pay attention to God's righteous judgment. If he does not accept the one who speaks against the righteous man on God's own behalf, will he accept those who speak against the righteous man contrary to justice? So he rebukes Job's friends and says: "And now, were it not for my servant Job, I would have destroyed you." He both rebukes and saves at the same time. He saves them because they said nothing wicked against God, and he rebukes the righteous man in correcting his simplicity. He honors the friends for Job's sake, and he honors the righteous man for his struggle. He gives him double, and out of his darkness the light shone, both then and now. Let us say one thing more and show how great the reward was. He received his sheep twice over, his oxen, camels and donkeys twice over; but having lost ten children, he did not receive twenty. Here we must ask why the animals were doubled but the children were not. It is because animals and possessions, once lost, perish completely, but a human being who dies is kept safe for life and raised up at the resurrection. He does not give him twice as many children, so as not to cut off hope for those who had departed, but to show him that they too, though snatched away before him, are alive. All of them are granted to him, yet he gives him only ten, so that Job might be found to pass not from life to death but from one house to another. For ten escorted him to the tomb when his life was finished, and ten more will welcome him from the tomb into the kingdom on the day of resurrection, and together they will enjoy those ineffable and eternal good things. May we all be counted worthy of them, by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and power, now and always and to the ages. Amen.
